summary: Adds a RObust Header Compression profile for compressing plain IP headers on their own, filling a gap left by the original ROHC framework in RFC 3095. That earlier document covered IP/UDP/RTP, IP/ESP and IP/UDP but not IP alone.

plainLanguage.summary: ROHC is a way of shrinking network headers by sending the parts that repeat only once and then sending only the changes. This document adds the missing piece: a profile that compresses plain IP headers, with no UDP or RTP involved, and that can handle any number of stacked IP headers.

subtitle: The missing ROHC profile: compressing plain IP headers on their own, with no UDP or RTP underneath.

tldr.problem: The original ROHC framework defines profiles for IP/UDP/RTP, IP/ESP and IP/UDP, plus one that compresses nothing. There is no profile for compressing a plain IP header, even though the IP header is often a large part of a packet.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines profile 0x0004, a simplified version of the IP/UDP profile with UDP removed. It changes how the static chain ends, adds a dynamic chain so that IP header chains of arbitrary length can be compressed, and adds a flag for a constant IP identifier.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Proposed Standard from June 2004 and was later updated by RFC 4815. It fills the gap the ROHC framework left open for IP-only traffic.

sections.title: The Missing Profile
sections.content:
The original RObust Header Compression RFC, RFC 3095, defines a framework for header compression along with compression protocols, called profiles, for IP/UDP/RTP, IP/ESP, IP/UDP and a profile for uncompressed packet streams. The uncompressed profile exists so that all traffic can be encapsulated over a link within ROHC packets, letting the lower layers avoid multiplexing different packet types. It is simple and can tunnel arbitrary packets, but it does not compress the headers at all.

Since normally all packets are expected to be IP packets, and the IP header often represents a major part of the total header, compression of the IP header alone would for most packets be a useful alternative to no compression. No such profile was defined in RFC 3095, and this has been identified as an important missing piece in the ROHC toolbox.

This document defines a ROHC compression profile for IP only, similar to the IP/UDP profile but simplified to exclude UDP. Because of the similarities with the IP/UDP profile, the IP compression profile is described based on that profile, mainly covering differences. The most important differences are a different way of terminating the static header chain and the capability of compressing IP header chains of arbitrary length. In general there are no major differences between the two profiles, since removing UDP has no impact on the compression mechanisms in principle. As in the IP/UDP profile, the compressor generates a 16-bit sequence number that increases by one for each packet compressed in the stream.
sections.plainLanguage: ROHC shrinks headers by sending the repeating parts once and then only the differences. The framework had profiles for IP/UDP/RTP, IP/ESP and IP/UDP, but none for plain IP. This one fills that hole.

sections.title: Profile 0x0004 and Static Chain Termination
sections.content:
In the IP profile defined here, known as ROHC IP, the static chain is terminated when the "Next Header / Protocol" field of a static IP header part indicates anything but IP, that is, anything other than IPinIP or IPv6. Alternatively, the compressor can choose to end the static chain at any IP header and indicate this by setting the most significant bit of the IP version field to 1, which is the value 0xC for IPv4 or 0xE for IPv6. The decompressor must store this indication in the context for correct decompression of subsequent headers, and the IP version field in decompressed headers must be restored to its original value.

This is the first of the two important differences from the IP/UDP profile. In the UDP profile the chain always ends with a UDP header part, which by definition provides the boundary for the chain, and the UDP header is also the last header in the uncompressed packet, apart from a possible application header. For the IP-only profile there is no single last header that ends the chain by definition, so the profile needs another way to mark the end.
sections.plainLanguage: A compressed header normally ends at a known point, such as the UDP header. With plain IP there is no such fixed point, so the chain ends either at a header that is not followed by another IP header, or at a header marked with a special version value.

sections.title: Header Chains of Arbitrary Length
sections.content:
In the profiles defined by RFC 3095, there is a single last header in the header chain that marks the end of the static chain, and the length of the dynamic chain is then inferred from the static chain in the IR header or from the static chain in the context for the IR-DYN header. Both chains may be of arbitrary length, so a context may in theory be initialized with an arbitrary number of IP levels. However, the general compressed header formats of RFC 3095 allow at most two levels of IP headers, the inner and the outer, in a compressed header, and list compression cannot be used for additional IP headers. The consequence for the RFC 3095 profiles is that at most two levels of IP headers can be compressed; extra IP headers at best partially disable header compression, and the compressor is then only allowed to send IR and IR-DYN packets.

For IP-only compression, additional IP headers would not have to disable header compression, because there is no single packet type that ends the compressed chain. The excess IP headers could simply be left uncompressed by implicitly terminating the static and dynamic chains after at most two levels. The IP-only profile goes one step further and supports compression of an arbitrary number of IP levels. This is achieved by adding a dynamic chain to the general format of compressed headers, holding the header part of each IP level in excess of the first two. The information related to the initial two IP headers is carried as for the IP/UDP profile, and a chain of dynamic header information is added to the end of the compressed header for every additional IP header. The length of the chain is inferred from the chain of static parameters in the context. While a dynamic chain carries dynamically changing parameters using an uncompressed representation, this ensures that flows with arbitrary levels of IP headers will not impair compression efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: The older profiles could only squeeze two IP headers into one packet, so extra headers made compression useless. This profile adds a list of extra header parts to the compressed packet, so a tunnel of any depth still compresses well.

sections.title: The Constant IP-ID
sections.content:
Most IPv4 stacks assign an IP-ID according to the value of a counter that increases by one for each outgoing packet. ROHC UDP compresses the IP-ID field using offset IP-ID encoding based on the UDP sequence number. For stacks generating IP-ID values using a pseudo-random number generator, the field is not compressed and is sent as is, in its entirety, as additional octets after the compressed header. Cases have also been found where an IPv4 stack uses a constant value for the IP Identifier. When the IP-ID field is constant it cannot be compressed using offset IP-ID encoding, so the field must be sent in its entirety.

This overhead is avoided with the addition of a flag within the dynamic part of the chain used to initialize the IPv4 header. The dynamic part carries the Type of Service and Time to Live octets, then the two-octet Identification field, then a row of flags: DF, RND, NBO, SID and a reserved zero bit. SID means static IP identifier. For IR and IR-DYN packets the logic is the same as for ROHC UDP with the addition that the SID field must be kept in the context. For compressed headers other than IR and IR-DYN, if the RND value is 0 and the context SID is 0, the IP-ID is compressed using offset IP-ID encoding with p = 0 and a default slope of 0. If the RND value is 0 and the context SID is 1, the IP-ID is constant and compressed away, and its value is the context IP-ID. If the RND value is 1, the IP-ID is the uncompressed value and is passed as additional octets at the end of the compressed header, after any extensions. Only IR and IR-DYN packets can update the context SID.
sections.plainLanguage: Some stacks keep the same IP identification number for every packet. The IP-only profile adds one flag that tells the other end to keep that number instead of sending it again with each packet.

sections.title: Canceling a Mode Transition
sections.content:
The profiles defined in RFC 3095 operate in different modes of compression: Unidirectional, Bi-directional Optimistic and Bi-directional Reliable. Compression always starts in Unidirectional mode, and mode transitions can only be initiated by the decompressor, which requests a transition once a packet has reached it. The compressor is compelled to honor such requests.

For the IP profile, the Mode parameter value of 0, used with the UOR-2, IR and IR-DYN packet types, is redefined to let the compressor decline a requested mode transition. Upon receiving the Mode parameter set to 0, the decompressor MUST stay in its current mode of operation and SHOULD refrain from sending further mode transition requests for the declined mode for a certain amount of time.

The RFC then sets out how the four state variables behave. On the compressor side, the mode value must not change when sending mode information within packets if the mode parameter is set to 0, and the transition flag is pending when a mode transition request is received from the decompressor, becoming done when the compressor receives an acknowledgement for a UOR-2, IR-DYN or IR packet sent with the mode parameter set to the mode in use when the request was initiated. On the decompressor side, the mode MUST remain unchanged when receiving a UOR-2, IR-DYN or IR packet sent with the mode parameter set to 0, and the transition flag is pending on receipt, becoming done when a packet of the corresponding type for the unchanged mode is received. Appendix A gives the detailed procedures for canceling a transition from Optimistic to Reliable mode, from Unidirectional to Reliable mode, from Reliable to Optimistic mode, and back to Unidirectional mode.
sections.plainLanguage: The decompressor normally asks the compressor to switch mode and the compressor must agree. This profile lets the compressor say no, and the decompressor has to stay in its current mode until it asks again later.

sections.title: Packet Types, Initialization and the Compressed Format
sections.content:
Except for one new feedback option, the only packet format that differs from ROHC UDP is the general format for compressed packets, which has no UDP checksum at the end. Instead it ends with a list of dynamic header portions, one for each IP header above the initial two, if any, as indicated by the presence of corresponding header portions in the static chain. The general format runs from the Add-CID octet and the base header, through the optional CID, the remainder of the base header and any extension, then the IP-ID of the outer IPv4 header, the outer list's AH data and GRE checksum, the IP-ID of the inner IPv4 header, the inner list's AH data and GRE checksum, and finally the list of dynamic chains for the additional IP headers, whose length is given by the static chain and which include no sequence number. The sequence number is present within compressed base headers.

The static context for ROHC IP compression can be initialized in two ways. It can be initialized by using an IR packet as in ROHC UDP, where the profile is 0x0004 and the static chain ends with the static part of an IP header whose Next Header or Protocol field has any value except IPinIP (4) or IPv6 (41), or where the IP version field indicates termination. It can also be initialized by reusing an existing context, done with an IR-DYN packet identifying profile 0x0004, where the dynamic chain corresponds to the prefix of the existing static chain. In both cases the sequence number is initialized to a random value when the first IR or IR-DYN packet is sent.

The new CONTEXT_MEMORY feedback option informs the compressor that the decompressor does not have sufficient memory resources to handle the context of the packet stream as it is currently compressed. Its option type is 9 and its option length is 0. On receiving it, the compressor SHOULD take actions to compress the packet stream in a way that requires fewer decompressor memory resources, or stop compressing the packet stream.
sections.plainLanguage: The compressed packet keeps the usual shape but drops the UDP checksum and adds the extra header parts at the end. A context is set up either from scratch or by reusing an existing one. A new feedback option lets the decompressor say that it is running out of memory.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says that the security considerations of RFC 3095 apply equally to this document, without exceptions or additions. The profile is a compression format and adds no new mechanism of its own: it reuses the framework, its modes of operation and its feedback options, and changes only how the header chain ends and how constant IP identifiers are signalled.
sections.plainLanguage: This document adds nothing new about security. Whatever the ROHC framework in RFC 3095 says about security applies here unchanged.
